mainEntity.name: What is a cryptographic hash function?

acceptedAnswer.text: A cryptographic hash function maps an input of any size to a fixed-length digest. It is deterministic, one-way (pre-image resistant), and collision resistant — making it infeasible to reverse the output or find two inputs that produce the same hash.

MD5 is cryptographically broken for collision resistance. Practical collision attacks have been demonstrated, and it should not be used for digital signatures or security-critical applications. It remains widely used for non-security checksums and data integrity verification where collision resistance is not required.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between MD2, MD4, and MD5?

acceptedAnswer.text: MD2 (1989) is the oldest and slowest, designed for 8-bit machines. MD4 (1990) introduced a faster design but was quickly found to be weak. MD5 (1991) is the most widely used variant, producing a 128-bit digest, though it is now considered cryptographically broken for collision resistance.

mainEntity.name: Are MD5 hashes safe for passwords?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. MD5 is designed to be fast, which makes it unsuitable for password storage. Use a slow, purpose-built algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 instead.

mainEntity.name: How does MD5Kit protect my data?

acceptedAnswer.text: All hashing runs entirely inside your browser. MD4 and MD5 use hash-wasm (a WebAssembly library loaded from CDN), and MD2 uses a custom inlined RFC 1319 implementation. No text, file content, or hash output is ever transmitted to any server.
